The Committee’s move to lower the funds rate and maintain ample reserves points to a cautiously supportive stance: it aims to bolster activity amid low inflation and soft external demand while acknowledging persistent uncertainties. The explicit weakness in business fixed investment is notable because research shows investment is highly sensitive to internal finance and credit conditions—inventory and fixed investment tend to contract when financing is tight (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994), tempering the growth impulse even with lower policy rates.

With inflation running below 2% and market-based compensation subdued, the outlook is consistent with evidence from New Keynesian Phillips curve estimates (e.g., Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido) that anchored expectations and modest slack can keep inflation muted despite a strong labor market. Monetary policy can support real activity (Sims; B. Friedman; McCallum and Nelson, 1999), and the Desk’s T-bill purchases and repo operations should stabilize money markets and facilitate transmission. Still, the combination of weak investment and global headwinds justifies a more guarded tone than a purely upbeat one. Overall assessment: cautiously positive.
